content: Astigmatism is an optical condition where an optical system has different focal points for light rays traveling in two perpendicular planes. This results in images that are not uniformly focused. For example, if an optical system with astigmatism is used to image a cross, the vertical and horizontal lines of the cross will come into sharp focus at different distances. There are two main types of astigmatism. The first type is a third-order aberration, which occurs for objects or parts of objects that are located away from the optical axis. This type of astigmatism can occur even in perfectly symmetrical optical systems and is often referred to as a monochromatic aberration because it can occur with light of a single wavelength. However, the degree of this aberration can vary significantly depending on the wavelength of light. The second type of astigmatism arises when the optical system lacks symmetry about the optical axis. This asymmetry may be intentional, such as in the design of cylindrical lenses, or it may result from manufacturing defects or misalignment of optical components. This form of astigmatism is particularly relevant in ophthalmology, as it is commonly caused by irregularities in the shape of the cornea or lens of the human eye. In third-order astigmatism, light rays from a single point on an object propagate in two specific planes: the tangential plane and the sagittal plane. The tangential plane includes the object point and the optical axis, and rays traveling in this plane are called tangential rays. The sagittal plane, on the other hand, is orthogonal to the tangential plane and intersects the optical axis at the entrance pupil of the system. Rays in this plane are referred to as sagittal rays. In this type of astigmatism, the tangential and sagittal rays come to focus at different points along the optical axis, known as the tangential focus and sagittal focus, respectively. At the tangential focus, the image appears as a short line oriented in the sagittal direction, while at the sagittal focus, the image appears as a short line oriented in the tangential direction. Between these two foci, a circular but blurry image is formed, known as the circle of least confusion or medial focus. This plane often represents the best compromise for image clarity in systems with astigmatism. The severity of third-order astigmatism increases with the square of the angle between the object rays and the optical axis. Optical systems can be designed to minimize or eliminate astigmatism, and such systems are referred to as anastigmats. Astigmatism can also occur in optical systems that are not rotationally symmetric. This may result from errors in the shape of optical surfaces or misalignment of components. In some cases, this type of astigmatism is intentionally introduced, such as in certain telescope designs. In these systems, tangential rays and sagittal rays are analyzed to understand the effects of astigmatism. In ophthalmology, astigmatism is a refractive error of the eye where the degree of refraction differs between the vertical and horizontal meridians, referred to as the tangential and sagittal meridians, respectively. This condition is often caused by an irregularly shaped cornea, where the curvature and refractive power differ between meridians. Astigmatism can impair the ability to see fine details and may cause vertical lines or objects to appear tilted. It is a common condition, affecting approximately one in three individuals, and its prevalence increases with age. Mild astigmatism may go unnoticed, but more severe cases can lead to blurry vision, squinting, eye strain, fatigue, or headaches. Astigmatism can be corrected using glasses with cylindrical lenses, contact lenses, or refractive surgery. To diagnose astigmatism, ophthalmologists and optometrists use various tests during eye examinations. A Snellen chart or similar eye chart may reveal reduced visual acuity. A clock dial or sunburst chart may also be used to determine the axis and power of astigmatism. Astigmatism can also result from misaligned or malformed lenses and mirrors during the manufacturing process. If these distortions are not corrected, they can become permanently polished into the surface, leading to astigmatic errors. These errors are more pronounced in optical components with high aspect ratios (diameter-to-thickness ratios). Proper support and careful manufacturing techniques are essential to minimize such distortions. In some optical systems, astigmatism is deliberately introduced for specific purposes. For example, compact disc players use an astigmatic lens for focusing. When one axis is more in focus than the other, the dot-like features on the disc appear as ovals, and the orientation of the oval indicates which axis requires adjustment. This information is used to fine-tune the lens position for optimal focus. Similarly, some telescopes incorporate astigmatic optics for specific design advantages.
